questions.title: What is scope in Python?
questions.answer: Scope defines the region of a program where a variable or name can be accessed. Python has four main scopes: Local, Enclosing, Global and Built-in. Python follows the LEGB rule to resolve variable names.

questions.title: What are the four types of scope in Python?
questions.answer: Python has four types of scope: 1. Local: Variables defined inside a function. 2. Enclosing: Variables defined in an outer function. 3. Global: Variables defined at the module level. 4. Built-in: Names provided by Python, such as `print()`, `len()` and `sum()`.

questions.title: What is local scope?
questions.answer: A variable created inside a function belongs to its local scope. It can normally be accessed only inside that function.
questions.code:
def greet():
    message = "Hello"

print(message)

greet()

# Hello#

print(message)

# NameError

questions.title: What is global scope?
questions.answer: A variable defined at the module level has global scope. It can be accessed inside functions, provided there isn't a conflicting local binding.
questions.code:
name = "Abhiraj"
def greet():

print(name)

greet()

# Abhiraj

questions.title: What is enclosing scope?
questions.answer: Enclosing scope occurs when we define a function inside another function. The inner function can access variables from its outer function.

questions.title: What is built-in scope?
questions.answer: Built-in scope contains predefined Python names available without importing anything, such as `print()`, `len()`, `range()`, `list()` and `Exception`.
questions.code:
numbers = [10, 20, 30]

print(len(numbers)

)

questions.title: Can a local variable have the same name as a global variable?
questions.answer: Yes. Python allows it. The local variable shadows the global variable inside that function.
questions.code:

questions.title: What is variable shadowing?
questions.answer: Variable shadowing happens when a variable in an inner scope uses the same name as a variable in an outer scope. The inner variable takes precedence when resolving that name.

questions.title: What happens when a function accesses a global variable without modifying it?
questions.answer: Python can directly access the global variable without using the `global` keyword, as long as we only read it.
questions.code:
count = 10
def show():

print(count)

show()

questions.title: Are variables declared inside an if block local to that block?
questions.answer: No. Python does not create a separate scope for `if`, `for` or `while` blocks. Variables assigned inside these blocks belong to the surrounding scope.
questions.code:
if True:    x = 100

print(x)

# 100

questions.title: Does a loop create a new scope in Python?
questions.answer: No. Unlike some other programming languages, Python loops do not introduce a separate local scope.
questions.code:
for i in range(3):    pass

print(i)

# 2

questions.title: Does a function create a new scope?
questions.answer: Yes. Every function invocation creates a new local execution environment. Its local variables are independent of other function calls.

questions.title: Can nested functions access variables from their parent function?
questions.answer: Yes. Inner functions can read variables from enclosing functions because Python searches the enclosing scope during name resolution.

questions.title: What happens to local variables after a function finishes execution?
questions.answer: Their local references are released when the function's execution frame is destroyed. However, objects referenced by those variables may remain alive if other references exist, such as a returned closure.

questions.title: Can two functions have local variables with the same name?
questions.answer: Yes. Each function has its own local scope, so the same variable name can exist independently in multiple functions.

questions.title: What is the difference between scope and lifetime?
questions.answer: Scope determines where a variable can be accessed, whereas lifetime determines how long the object or reference exists in memory. They are related but not identical.

questions.title: Can a function access a variable defined in another unrelated function?
questions.answer: Not directly. If the functions don't share an enclosing scope or another reference to the variable, it isn't accessible by its local name. We can pass it as an argument or return it.

questions.answer: Python provides `locals()` and `globals()`.

questions.title: What is the LEGB rule?
questions.answer: Python follows the LEGB rule. It searches for a name in this order: 1. Local 2. Enclosing 3. Global 4. Built-in It stops when it finds the name.

questions.title: Explain LEGB with an example.
questions.answer: Python finds `x` in the local scope first, so it doesn't search the remaining scopes.
questions.code:
x = "Global"

def outer():
    x = "Enclosing"
    def inner():
        x = "Local"
        print(x)
    inner()

outer()

questions.title: What happens if a variable is not found in any LEGB scope?
questions.answer: Python raises a `NameError` because it cannot resolve the requested name.

questions.title: Does Python always follow LEGB?
questions.answer: Yes, for ordinary lexical name resolution in Python functions. However, class namespaces have some special rules and aren't treated as ordinary enclosing function scopes.

questions.title: What is name resolution?
questions.answer: Name resolution is the process Python uses to identify which object a variable or name refers to when the program executes.

questions.title: What is lexical scoping?
questions.answer: Lexical scoping means the accessibility of variables is determined by where functions are defined in the source code, not where they are called.

questions.title: Does calling a function from another function change its enclosing scope?
questions.answer: No. A function's lexical enclosing scope is determined by its definition location, not its caller.

questions.title: Can the same name refer to different objects in different scopes?
questions.answer: Yes. Each scope can bind the same name to a different object. Python resolves the name according to the LEGB rule.

questions.title: What is the difference between globals() and locals()?
questions.answer: `globals()` returns the module's global namespace dictionary, while `locals()` returns the current local namespace mapping. Their behaviour differs depending on the execution scope, and modifying the dictionary returned by `locals()` inside an optimized function is not a reliable way to modify local variables.

questions.title: What is the global keyword?
questions.answer: The `global` keyword tells Python that a name inside a function refers to a module-level global variable rather than creating a new local binding.

questions.title: Why do we need the global keyword?
questions.answer: We need it when we want to reassign a global variable inside a function.
questions.code:
count = 10
def update():
    global count    count = 20update()
print(count)

# 20

questions.title: What happens if we modify a global variable without using global?
questions.answer: If we assign to the name inside a function, Python treats it as local by default. This can cause an `UnboundLocalError` when we try to read it before assignment.
questions.code:
x = 10
def test():

print(x)

    x = 20test()

questions.title: Why does Python raise UnboundLocalError instead of NameError?
questions.answer: Because Python has determined that `x` is a local variable in that function due to the assignment. However, we try to access it before it has been initialized.

questions.title: Can we use global for multiple variables?
questions.answer: Yes.
questions.code:
x = 10
y = 20
def update():
    global x, y    x = 100    y = 200

questions.title: Can we declare a global variable inside a nested function?
questions.answer: Yes. The `global` keyword always refers to the module-level namespace, not the enclosing function.

questions.title: Does global create a variable?
questions.answer: The declaration itself doesn't create a variable. It tells Python how to resolve assignments to that name. An assignment can then bind the name in the module namespace.

questions.title: Can we use global to modify mutable objects?
questions.answer: We don't need `global` if we only mutate the object without rebinding its name.
questions.code:

def add_item():

questions.title: Do we need global when reassigning a mutable object?
questions.answer: Yes. Rebinding a global variable requires `global`, even if the object is mutable.

questions.title: What is the difference between modifying and rebinding a variable?
questions.answer: Modifying means changing the existing object's contents. Rebinding means making a variable refer to another object.
questions.code:
items = [1, 2]
items.append(3)

# Mutationitems = [4, 5]   # Rebinding

questions.title: Can global variables create problems in large applications?
questions.answer: Yes. They introduce shared mutable state, making testing, debugging, concurrency and maintenance harder. Dependency injection, function arguments and dedicated state-management objects are often better alternatives.

questions.title: Can we declare the same name as both global and local in one function?
questions.answer: No. Declaring a name as global and then using it as a local variable in the same scope creates a syntax error.

questions.title: What is the nonlocal keyword?
questions.answer: The `nonlocal` keyword tells Python that a variable inside a nested function belongs to an enclosing function scope. It allows us to reassign that variable without creating a new local variable.

questions.title: Why do we need nonlocal?
questions.answer: We use it when an inner function needs to modify a variable belonging to its outer function.
questions.code:
def outer():
    count = 0
def inner():
    nonlocal count        count += 1    inner()

print(count)

outer()

questions.title: What is the difference between global and nonlocal?
questions.answer:

| ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| Refers to module-level variables         | Refers to enclosing function variables   |
| Used for global reassignment             | Used for enclosing variable reassignment |
| Doesn't require an enclosing function    | Requires an enclosing function binding   |
| Can be used at module and function scope | Used inside nested function scopes       |

questions.title: Can nonlocal access a global variable?
questions.answer: No. `nonlocal` searches enclosing function scopes. It doesn't refer to the module-level global scope.

questions.title: What happens if a nonlocal variable doesn't exist?
questions.answer: Python raises a `SyntaxError` because it cannot find an existing binding in any enclosing function scope.

questions.title: Can we use nonlocal in a function without nesting?
questions.answer: No. There must be an enclosing function scope containing the referenced variable.

questions.title: Can nonlocal modify multiple variables?
questions.answer: Yes.

questions.title: Can nonlocal be used with mutable objects?
questions.answer: Yes, but it isn't required just to mutate an existing object. It is needed when rebinding the enclosing variable.

questions.title: What is the practical use of nonlocal?
questions.answer: It is useful for closures, counters, stateful functions and function factories where an inner function needs to maintain and update state.

questions.title: What happens when global and nonlocal are declared for the same name?
questions.answer: Python raises a `SyntaxError`. A name cannot simultaneously refer to a global and a nonlocal binding within the same scope.

questions.title: What are first-class functions in Python?
questions.answer: It means functions are treated like ordinary objects in Python. We can assign them to variables, pass them as arguments, return them from other functions and store them in data structures.

questions.title: Are functions objects in Python?
questions.answer: Yes. A function is an object of type `function`. It has attributes, can be assigned to variables and can be passed around like other objects.

questions.title: Can we assign a function to another variable?
questions.answer: Yes. Both variables can refer to the same function object.
questions.code:
def greet():

print("Hello")

welcome = greetwelcome()

# Hello

questions.title: What is the difference between greet and greet()?
questions.answer: `greet` refers to the function object, whereas `greet()` calls the function and evaluates its return value.
questions.code:

    return "Hello"

print(greet)

# Function object

print(greet()

)

questions.title: Can we store functions inside a list?
questions.answer: Yes. Since functions are objects, we can store them in lists, tuples and dictionaries.

questions.title: Can a function be passed as an argument?
questions.answer: Yes. We can pass a function as an argument to another function. This is one of the foundations of higher-order functions.

questions.title: Can a function return another function?
questions.answer: Yes. Python allows functions to return other functions because functions are first-class objects.

questions.title: What is the difference between returning a function and calling a function?
questions.answer: Returning a function gives us the function object, while calling a function executes it and returns its result.

questions.title: Can we attach attributes to functions?
questions.answer: Yes. Python functions generally allow custom attributes.
questions.code:
def greet():
    passgreet.role = "Admin"

print(greet.role)

questions.title: What is the difference between a function and a method?
questions.answer: A function is a callable object that can be called independently. A method is a function associated with an object or class. When accessed through an instance, a normal instance method is bound to that instance.

questions.title: What is a bound method?
questions.answer: A bound method is a method associated with a particular instance. Python automatically passes that instance as the first argument, conventionally named `self`.

questions.title: What is the difference between a function and a callable?
questions.answer: A function is a specific kind of callable. A callable is any object that supports the `__call__()` method.

questions.title: How can you check whether an object is callable?
questions.answer: We can use Python's built-in `callable()` function.

questions.title: Why are first-class functions important in Python?
questions.answer: They make functional programming, decorators, callbacks, closures, dependency injection and reusable abstractions possible.

questions.title: What is a higher-order function?
questions.answer: A higher-order function is a function that either accepts another function as an argument or returns a function as its result.

questions.title: What is a callback function?
questions.answer: A callback is a function passed to another function so that it can be executed at an appropriate time.

questions.title: What is the difference between a callback and a higher-order function?
questions.answer: A higher-order function is the function that accepts or returns another function. A callback is the function passed to it for execution.

questions.title: Explain function composition.
questions.answer: Function composition means combining multiple functions so that the output of one function becomes the input of another.

questions.title: What is map()?
questions.answer: `map()` applies a function to every element of an iterable and returns a map iterator.

questions.answer: `filter()` selects elements from an iterable for which the given function returns a truthy value.

result = filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0, numbers)

questions.title: Are map and filter lazy?
questions.answer: Yes. They return iterators and perform their operations when values are requested rather than immediately creating a complete result list.

questions.title: What happens if we iterate over a map iterator twice?
questions.answer: The second iteration produces no values because iterators are generally consumed as they are traversed.

questions.title: Can map accept multiple iterables?
questions.answer: Yes. The function receives corresponding elements from each iterable as positional arguments. Iteration stops when the shortest iterable is exhausted.

questions.title: What is the difference between map and list comprehension?
questions.answer: Both can transform iterable elements. `map()` accepts a function and returns an iterator, whereas list comprehension directly constructs a list. List comprehensions are often more readable for simple transformations.

questions.title: When would you prefer a generator expression over map?
questions.answer: When I want lazy evaluation and a readable expression without necessarily creating a separate function. The choice depends on readability and the transformation complexity.

questions.title: Are higher-order functions useful in backend development?
questions.answer: Yes. They are useful for middleware, callbacks, validation pipelines, reusable business logic, event handling and decorators.

questions.title: What is a closure in Python?
questions.answer: A closure is a function that remembers and accesses variables from its enclosing scope even after the outer function has finished executing. For example, imagine a bank account. We create an account with an initial balance, and the returned function remembers that balance.

questions.title: What are the three important conditions for a closure?
questions.answer: Generally, a closure involves: 1. A nested function. 2. The inner function references a variable from its enclosing function. 3. The outer function returns or otherwise allows the inner function to survive beyond the outer function's execution.

questions.title: Why does a closure remember variables after the outer function finishes?
questions.answer: Python keeps the necessary enclosing bindings alive because the inner function still references them. These references are stored in the function's closure cells.

questions.title: How can we inspect a closure?
questions.answer: We can inspect the `__closure__` attribute of a function and examine its cell contents.

questions.title: What is __closure__?
questions.answer: `__closure__` is an attribute containing the closure cells associated with a function. It is `None` when the function has no closure cells.

questions.title: What is a closure cell?
questions.answer: A closure cell is an internal object used to hold a reference to a variable captured from an enclosing scope. It allows the inner function to access that variable later.

questions.title: Can a closure modify an enclosing variable?
questions.answer: Yes. We can use `nonlocal` to reassign the enclosing variable.

questions.title: Why are closures useful?
questions.answer: Closures are useful when we want to maintain state without creating a class, implement decorators, create function factories and encapsulate data within a function.

questions.title: What is a stateful closure?
questions.answer: A stateful closure maintains data between multiple function calls using variables captured from its enclosing scope.

questions.title: Can we create multiple independent closures from the same outer function?
questions.answer: Yes. Every call to the outer function creates a separate enclosing execution environment.

questions.title: What is late binding in closures?
questions.answer: Late binding means that a closure resolves the value of a captured variable when the inner function executes, rather than freezing the variable's value when the closure is created.
questions.code:
functions = []
for i in range(3):
    functions.append(lambda: i)

print([f() for f in functions])

questions.title: How do you fix late binding in closures?
questions.answer: One common solution is to use a default argument to capture the current value when the lambda is created.
questions.code:
functions = []for i in range(3):    functions.append(lambda i=i: i)

print([f()

 for f in functions])

# [0, 1, 2]

questions.title: Why does using a default argument fix late binding?
questions.answer: Default argument expressions are evaluated when the function is defined. Therefore, each lambda gets its own default value for `i`.

questions.title: Can closures capture mutable objects?
questions.answer: Yes. Closures can capture references to mutable objects. If that object changes, the closure can observe those changes.

questions.title: Is a closure the same as a global variable?
questions.answer: No. A closure captures variables from an enclosing function scope, whereas a global variable belongs to the module namespace. Closures are useful for maintaining isolated state.

questions.title: Can closures be used for data hiding?
questions.answer: Yes. Closures can provide a form of encapsulation because external code cannot directly access the enclosing local variable by its original name.

questions.title: Can a closure return another closure?
questions.answer: Yes. Functions can be nested and returned at multiple levels. Each closure can capture variables from its enclosing scopes.

questions.title: What is a function factory?
questions.answer: A function factory is a function that creates and returns another function, often using closures to customize its behaviour.

questions.title: What is the difference between closure and decorator?
questions.answer: A closure is a function that retains access to enclosing variables. A decorator is a callable that takes another callable and returns a replacement or wrapper. Decorators commonly use closures to remember the original function.

questions.title: Can closures cause memory-related issues?
questions.answer: Yes. A closure may keep referenced objects alive longer than expected. If it captures large objects or participates in reference cycles, memory usage can increase.

questions.title: Can two closures share the same enclosing variable?
questions.answer: Yes. If two inner functions are created within the same enclosing function execution, they can reference the same closure cell.

questions.title: What happens if the captured variable is reassigned after creating a closure?
questions.answer: If the enclosing scope reassigns the variable before the closure executes, the closure observes the updated binding.

questions.title: How are closures used in real-world applications?
questions.answer: They can be used for configurable validators, authorization checks, logging wrappers, caching, function factories and stateful callbacks.

questions.title: How would you explain closures in one minute during an interview?
questions.answer: "A closure is a function that remembers variables from its enclosing scope even after the outer function has completed execution. It works because Python retains the necessary variable bindings in closure cells. Closures are useful for data encapsulation, maintaining state, creating function factories and implementing decorators. One important concept related to closures is late binding, where captured variables are resolved when the function executes rather than when it is created."

questions.title: What is a decorator in Python?
questions.answer: A decorator is a callable that takes another callable and returns a callable, usually to extend or modify its behaviour without changing its original source code.

questions.title: What is the basic syntax of a decorator?
questions.answer: A decorator takes a function, wraps its execution inside an inner wrapper function, and returns that wrapper. When the decorated function is called, the wrapper runs code before and after the original call.

questions.title: How do decorators work internally?

questions.title: What is a wrapper function?
questions.answer: A wrapper is a function defined inside a decorator that adds behaviour before or after calling the original function. It can also modify arguments or return values.

questions.title: Why do decorators use *args and kwargs?
questions.answer: They allow the wrapper to accept different positional and keyword arguments, making the decorator reusable across functions with different signatures.

questions.title: Why should a wrapper return the original function's result?
questions.answer: If the wrapper doesn't return the result, the decorated function may unexpectedly return `None`, even when the original function returns a value.

questions.title: What is functools.wraps()?
questions.answer: `functools.wraps()` is a decorator used inside another decorator to preserve important metadata from the original function, such as its name, documentation string, module and annotations.

questions.title: Why is functools.wraps() important?
questions.answer: Without `wraps()`, the decorated function's metadata may reflect the wrapper rather than the original function. This can cause confusion in debugging, documentation, introspection and tooling.

questions.title: What happens if we don't use functools.wraps()?
questions.answer: The decorated function may expose the wrapper's `__name__`, `__doc__` and other metadata instead of the original function's metadata.

questions.title: What does functools.wraps() actually preserve?
questions.answer: It uses `functools.update_wrapper()` internally to copy selected attributes from the original function to the wrapper and update the wrapper's `__dict__`. It also sets `__wrapped__` to reference the original callable.

questions.title: Can decorators accept arguments?
questions.answer: Yes. We create an outer function that accepts configuration arguments and returns the actual decorator.

questions.title: How many functions are generally involved in a decorator with arguments?
questions.answer: Usually three levels: 1. Outer function: Accepts decorator configuration. 2. Decorator function: Accepts the original function. 3. Wrapper function: Executes the original function with additional behaviour.

questions.title: Can we apply multiple decorators to one function?
questions.answer: Yes. Python supports stacking multiple decorators on a single function.

questions.title: In which order are multiple decorators applied?
questions.answer: Decorators are applied from the bottom upward. The decorator closest to the function is applied first.

questions.title: In which order do stacked wrappers execute?
questions.answer: The outermost wrapper starts first. It may then call the next wrapper, which eventually calls the original function.

questions.title: Can decorators modify function arguments?
questions.answer: Yes. A wrapper can inspect, validate or modify the arguments before forwarding them to the original function.

questions.title: Can decorators modify return values?
questions.answer: Yes. A decorator can capture the original result, transform it and return the modified result.

questions.title: Can a decorator prevent a function from executing?
questions.answer: Yes. The wrapper can decide not to call the original function, for example when authorization fails.

questions.title: Can decorators be applied to class methods?
questions.answer: Yes. Decorators can be applied to instance methods, class methods and static methods. Python also provides built-in decorators such as `@classmethod`, `@staticmethod` and `@property`.

questions.title: What is a real-world use case of decorators?
questions.answer: Common applications include: - Authentication and authorization. - Logging. - Execution time measurement. - Caching. - Input validation. - Retry mechanisms. - Rate limiting.

questions.title: How would you implement an execution-time decorator?
questions.answer: I use `time.perf_counter()` because it is suitable for measuring elapsed time with high resolution.

questions.title: How would you implement a caching decorator?
questions.answer: For simple caching, I can use Python's built-in `functools.lru_cache()` instead of implementing a cache manually.

questions.title: What is the difference between @staticmethod and @classmethod?
questions.answer:
| `staticmethod`                                        | `classmethod`                                                  |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Does not receive automatic instance or class argument | Receives the class as first argument                           |

questions.title: Can we decorate a class instead of a function?
questions.answer: Yes. A class decorator receives a class and returns a class, usually modified or replaced.

questions.title: What is the difference between a decorator and middleware?
questions.answer: A decorator wraps a callable to add behaviour. Middleware is an application-level processing component that intercepts requests and responses. Middleware can internally be implemented using callable wrappers or other mechanisms.

questions.title: Can decorators change the signature of a function?
questions.answer: Yes. A wrapper may have a different actual signature. `functools.wraps()` helps preserve metadata and exposes the original function through `__wrapped__`, which allows introspection tools to recover the original signature in many cases. For explicit signatures, additional techniques may be necessary.

questions.title: What is the difference between __name__ and __wrapped__?
questions.answer: `__name__` contains the function's name. `__wrapped__` points to the original wrapped callable when using `functools.wraps()`.

questions.title: What are the potential problems with decorators?
questions.answer: Poorly implemented decorators can hide function metadata, alter return values unexpectedly, make debugging harder, introduce performance overhead and create unexpected interactions when multiple decorators are stacked.

questions.title: Explain decorators in an actual backend application.
questions.answer: "In a backend application, I can use decorators to separate cross-cutting concerns from business logic. For example, an authorization decorator can verify whether a user has permission before executing a protected function. Similarly, logging and caching decorators can add reusable functionality without duplicating code in every endpoint or service."

questions.title: What is recursion?
questions.answer: Recursion is a programming technique in which a function calls itself to solve a problem by breaking it into smaller subproblems.

questions.title: What are the two essential parts of recursion?
questions.answer: Every recursive solution needs: 1. Base case: Stops further recursive calls. 2. Recursive case: Calls the function with a smaller or simpler problem.

questions.title: What happens internally when a recursive function is called?
questions.answer: Each function call creates a new execution frame containing information such as local variables, arguments and execution state. These frames are managed through the call stack.

questions.title: What is a call stack?
questions.answer: A call stack is a Last In, First Out structure used to track active function calls. When a function calls another function, a new frame is pushed. When execution returns, that frame is popped.

questions.title: Explain recursion using factorial.
questions.answer: The function keeps calling itself until it reaches the base case, and then the results are calculated while the calls return.

questions.title: What happens if a recursive function has no base case?
questions.answer: It may continue calling itself until Python reaches its recursion limit, resulting in a `RecursionError`.

questions.title: What is Python's recursion limit?
questions.answer: It is the maximum recursion depth Python allows before raising a `RecursionError`. We can inspect the current limit using `sys.getrecursionlimit()`.

questions.title: Can we increase the recursion limit?
questions.answer: Yes, using `sys.setrecursionlimit()`, but doing so carelessly can cause stack exhaustion or even crash the interpreter.

questions.title: Does Python support tail-call optimization?
questions.answer: No. Standard Python implementations such as CPython do not perform general tail-call optimization. Tail-recursive functions still consume recursion depth.

questions.title: What is tail recursion?
questions.answer: Tail recursion occurs when the recursive call is the final operation performed by a function, with no additional computation after it returns.

questions.title: What is the difference between recursion and iteration?
questions.answer:
| Recursion                        | Iteration                                        |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Function calls itself            | Uses loops                                       |
| Uses additional call frames      | Usually uses less call-stack space               |
| Can be elegant for tree problems | Often more memory-efficient                      |
| Can hit recursion limits         | Doesn't have the same recursion-depth limitation |

questions.title: Why can recursion be slower than iteration?
questions.answer: Recursion introduces function-call overhead and requires maintaining additional execution frames. Iteration can often perform the same task with less overhead.

questions.title: What is mutual recursion?
questions.answer: Mutual recursion occurs when two or more functions call each other.

questions.title: What is indirect recursion?
questions.answer: Indirect recursion occurs when a function calls another function that eventually calls the original function, either directly or through several functions.

questions.title: Why is naive Fibonacci recursion inefficient?
questions.answer: Because it recalculates the same subproblems multiple times, resulting in exponential time complexity.

questions.title: How can you optimize recursive Fibonacci?
questions.answer: We can use memoization to store previously calculated results.

questions.title: What are function annotations in Python?
questions.answer: Function annotations provide metadata about function parameters and return values. They are commonly used for type hints.
questions.code:
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a + b

questions.title: What does -> int mean?
questions.answer: It indicates that the function is expected to return an integer. However, Python does not automatically enforce this annotation at runtime.

questions.title: Are type hints mandatory in Python?
questions.answer: No. Python is dynamically typed, so type hints are optional.

questions.title: Does Python enforce type annotations automatically?
questions.answer: No. Python generally doesn't enforce function annotations at runtime. Static type checkers such as mypy and Pyright can inspect them.

questions.title: How can we inspect function annotations?
questions.answer: We can use the `__annotations__` attribute.

questions.title: What is the difference between type hints and type checking?
questions.answer: Type hints describe expected types, while type checking verifies whether the code follows those expectations. Type checking can be performed statically by external tools or explicitly at runtime.

questions.title: Can annotations contain types other than int and str?
questions.answer: Yes. They can contain classes, generic types, unions, callable types and other valid annotation expressions.

questions.title: How do you annotate a function that returns nothing?
questions.answer: We use `None` as the return annotation.
questions.code:
def greet(name: str) -> None:

print(name)

questions.title: How do you annotate an optional parameter?
questions.answer: We can use `Optional` or the union operator.
questions.code:
def greet(name: str | None = None) -> str:
    return name or "Guest"

questions.title: How do you annotate a function accepting a list of integers?
questions.answer: Refer to the code output and scope rules.
questions.code:
def calculate(numbers: list[int]) -> int:
    return sum(numbers)

questions.title: What is the difference between Any and object?
questions.answer: `Any` effectively disables many static type restrictions for that value. `object` represents any Python object but requires appropriate type narrowing or checks before accessing specific operations.

questions.title: What is a Callable annotation?
questions.answer: `Callable` is used to annotate objects that can be called, including functions.

questions.title: What is the difference between get_type_hints() and __annotations__?
questions.answer: `__annotations__` exposes the stored annotation mapping, while `typing.get_type_hints()` attempts to resolve forward references and evaluate annotations into their actual types.

questions.title: Why are annotations useful in backend development?
questions.answer: They improve readability, editor autocomplete, static analysis, API documentation and collaboration. Frameworks such as FastAPI also use type annotations to help define and validate API schemas.

questions.title: What is a partial function in Python?
questions.answer: A partial function is a callable created by fixing some arguments of an existing function. Python provides `functools.partial()` for this purpose.

questions.title: What is functools.partial()?
questions.answer: It allows us to create a new callable with some arguments already supplied.

questions.title: Why do we use partial functions?
questions.answer: They help reduce repetitive argument passing, create specialized functions and improve code reusability.

questions.title: Does partial execute the original function immediately?
questions.answer: No. It creates a new callable. The original function executes only when we call that new callable.

questions.title: Can partial fix positional arguments?
questions.answer: Yes.

questions.title: Can partial fix keyword arguments?
questions.answer: Yes.
questions.code:
from functools import partialdef greet

(name, message):

print(message, name)

say_hello = partial(greet, message="Hello")say_hello("Abhiraj")

questions.title: Can we combine positional and keyword arguments in partial?
questions.answer: Yes. We can provide both positional and keyword arguments.

questions.title: Can we override keyword arguments supplied to partial?
questions.answer: Yes. Keyword arguments passed during the eventual call override the corresponding keywords stored in the partial object.
questions.code:
from functools import partialdef greet

(name, message):

print(message, name)

hello = partial(greet, message="Hello")hello("Abhiraj", message="Welcome")

# Welcome Abhiraj

questions.title: Can positional arguments supplied later change the original argument order?
questions.answer: Yes, positional arguments are filled according to the original function's parameter order. Partial arguments occupy the earlier positional slots.
questions.code:
from functools import partialdef display

(a, b, c):

print(a, b, c)

func = partial(display, 10)func(20, 30)

# 10 20 30

questions.title: What is the difference between partial and lambda?
questions.answer: Both can create specialized callables. `partial()` is especially useful when we simply want to fix existing function arguments, whereas lambda allows us to define a new expression.

questions.title: What is the difference between partial and a decorator?
questions.answer: A partial fixes some arguments of a callable. A decorator wraps or replaces a callable to extend its behaviour.

questions.title: What are practical uses of partial in backend development?
questions.answer: It can be used for preconfigured API clients, logging functions, event handlers, callbacks and reusable validation functions.

questions.title: What is partialmethod()?
questions.answer: `functools.partialmethod()` is similar to `partial()`, but it is designed for defining partial methods inside classes.

questions.title: What is functional programming?
questions.answer: Functional programming is a programming paradigm that emphasizes functions, expression evaluation, avoiding unnecessary mutable state and composing smaller functions to solve larger problems.

questions.title: What are the main principles of functional programming?
questions.answer: Some important principles are: 1. Pure functions. 2. Immutability. 3. First-class and higher-order functions. 4. Function composition. 5. Avoiding unnecessary side effects. 6. Declarative programming.

questions.title: What is a pure function?
questions.answer: A pure function always produces the same output for the same input and has no observable side effects.
questions.code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

questions.title: What is an impure function?
questions.answer: An impure function may produce different outputs for the same input or modify external state.
questions.code:
count = 0
def increment():
    global count    count += 1
    return count

questions.title: What are side effects?
questions.answer: Side effects are changes or interactions outside the function's returned value, such as modifying global variables, writing files, printing output or making network requests.

questions.title: What is immutability?
questions.answer: Immutability means an object's value cannot be changed after creation. Python examples include integers, strings and tuples, although a tuple can contain mutable objects.

questions.title: Is Python a functional programming language?
questions.answer: Python is a multi-paradigm language. It supports procedural, object-oriented and functional programming, but it is not a purely functional language.

questions.title: What is lambda in Python?
questions.answer: A lambda is a small anonymous function defined using the `lambda` keyword. It can contain a single expression.
questions.code:
square = lambda x: x * x

print(square(5)

)

questions.title: What is the difference between lambda and def?
questions.answer: `def` is used to define a regular named function with multiple statements, while `lambda` creates an anonymous function containing a single expression.

questions.title: Can lambda contain multiple statements?
questions.answer: No. A lambda body is limited to a single expression, although that expression can be complex.

questions.title: Can lambda return a value?
questions.answer: Yes. The evaluated expression is automatically returned.
questions.code:
square = lambda x: x ** 2

print(square(4)

)

# 16

questions.title: What is the difference between map and filter in functional programming?
questions.answer: `map()` transforms elements, while `filter()` selects elements based on a condition.

questions.title: What is function composition?
questions.answer: It is the process of combining functions so that the output of one becomes the input of another.

questions.title: What is referential transparency?
questions.answer: An expression is referentially transparent if it can be replaced with its resulting value without changing the program's observable behaviour. Pure functions are an important foundation for this concept.

questions.title: What is the difference between declarative and imperative programming?
questions.answer: Imperative programming describes how to perform a task step by step. Declarative programming describes what result is needed, leaving more implementation details to the underlying operations.

questions.title: What is a generator expression?
questions.answer: A generator expression creates a lazy iterator that produces values on demand.
questions.code:
numbers = (x * x for x in range(5))

print(next(numbers)

)

# 0

print(next(numbers)

)

# 1

questions.title: What is the difference between a generator function and a normal function?
questions.answer: A generator function uses `yield` to produce values lazily. A normal function typically executes and returns a result using `return`.

questions.title: What is the difference between return and yield?
questions.answer:
| return                                 | yield                                   |
| -------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Returns a result and ends the function | Produces a value and suspends execution |
| Doesn't create a generator by itself   | Makes the function a generator function |
| Function execution finishes            | Function can resume later               |

questions.title: What is lazy evaluation?
questions.answer: Lazy evaluation means delaying computation until the result is actually needed. Generators, `map()` and `filter()` are examples of lazy evaluation.

questions.title: What are the advantages of functional programming?
questions.answer: It encourages reusable code, predictable functions, easier unit testing, reduced shared mutable state and clearer data transformations. It can be particularly useful in data processing and concurrent systems.

questions.title: What are mutable default arguments in Python?
questions.answer: Default argument values are evaluated only once when the function is defined, not every time it is called. If we use a mutable object such as a list, the same object is reused across function calls.
questions.code:
def add_item(item, items=[]):
    items.append(item)
    return items

print(add_item(10))
print(add_item(20))
print(add_item(30))

questions.title: Why are mutable default arguments dangerous?
questions.answer: Because modifications made during one function call can affect subsequent calls. This can introduce unexpected shared state and bugs.

questions.title: What is the recommended solution for mutable default arguments?
questions.answer: Use `None` as the default value and create a new mutable object inside the function.

questions.title: Are all default arguments evaluated at function definition time?
questions.answer: Yes. Default argument expressions are evaluated once when the function definition executes. This applies to mutable and immutable default values.

questions.title: What happens if we modify an immutable default argument?
questions.answer: Immutable objects cannot be modified in place. An assignment to the parameter simply rebinds the local parameter and doesn't change the original default object.

questions.title: What is the difference between *args and kwargs?
questions.answer: `*args` collects additional positional arguments into a tuple, while `**kwargs` collects additional keyword arguments into a dictionary.

questions.title: What is argument unpacking?
questions.answer: Argument unpacking means passing elements of an iterable or mapping as individual function arguments using `*` or `**`.

questions.title: What is the difference between positional and keyword arguments?
questions.answer: Positional arguments are matched to parameters according to their position. Keyword arguments are matched using parameter names.

questions.title: What are positional-only parameters?
questions.answer: Positional-only parameters must be supplied by position, not by keyword. Python uses `/` in the function signature to define them.

questions.title: What are keyword-only parameters?
questions.answer: Keyword-only parameters must be supplied using their parameter names. We define them using `*` in the function signature.

questions.title: Can a Python function have both positional-only and keyword-only parameters?
questions.answer: Yes. Python supports positional-only, positional-or-keyword, variadic positional, keyword-only and variadic keyword parameters.

questions.title: What happens if we pass more positional arguments than a function accepts?
questions.answer: Python raises a `TypeError`, unless the function accepts additional positional arguments using `*args`.

questions.title: What happens if we pass an unexpected keyword argument?
questions.answer: Python raises a `TypeError`, unless the function accepts arbitrary keyword arguments using `**kwargs`.

questions.title: What is a function object in Python?
questions.answer: A function object contains references to its code, global namespace, defaults, metadata and other information required to execute it.

questions.title: What is __code__?
questions.answer: It is an attribute that provides access to a function's code object, containing compiled bytecode and information about its execution.
questions.code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

print(add.__code__.co_varnames)

# ('a', 'b')

questions.title: What is __globals__?
questions.answer: It provides access to the global namespace dictionary associated with a function.
questions.code:
x = 100
def show():

print(x)

print(show.__globals__["x"])

# 100

questions.title: What is __defaults__?
questions.answer: It stores the positional parameter default values of a function as a tuple, or `None` when there are no such defaults.
questions.code:
def greet(name="Guest", age=20):
    pass

print(greet.__defaults__)

# ('Guest', 20)

questions.title: What is the difference between __defaults__ and __kwdefaults__?
questions.answer: `__defaults__` stores defaults for positional parameters, while `__kwdefaults__` stores defaults for keyword-only parameters.
questions.code:
def example(a=10, *, b=20):
    pass

print(example.__defaults__)

print(example.__kwdefaults__)

questions.title: What is bytecode in Python?
questions.answer: Bytecode is an intermediate instruction representation generated when Python compiles source code. CPython executes this bytecode using its virtual machine.

questions.title: How can you inspect Python bytecode?
questions.answer: We can use the built-in `dis` module.

questions.title: What is the difference between compile time and runtime in Python?
questions.answer: During compilation, Python parses source code and generates code objects containing bytecode. At runtime, the interpreter executes that code. Some errors, such as syntax errors, are detected during compilation, while others occur during execution.

questions.title: Can functions be dynamically created or modified at runtime?
questions.answer: Yes. Python supports dynamic behaviour. We can create functions using `def` or `lambda`, attach attributes to function objects, assign functions to variables and replace references to existing functions. However, modifying a function's internals requires care.
